parsed.hook: At $14.56 at the LCBO, this old-vine blend from Roussillon undercuts most regional equivalents by half. The Tessellae combines Carignan, Syrah, Garnacha, and Monastrell from vines averaging 40+ years on schistose slopes above the Têt valley — a combination of grape variety and geology you rarely find at this price point.
parsed.wine_summary: Lafage has built a reputation in Roussillon by working cooperatively with small growers rather than owning extensive estate vineyards, which keeps quality high while prices accessible. The Côtes Catalanes appellation covers 118 communes in the Pyrénées-Orientales, a region where Mediterranean heat meets cooling altitude breezes from the Pyrenees, allowing grapes to ripen fully while retaining balancing acidity. The Vieilles Vignes designation signals that at least some parcels exceed 30 years of age, and old-vine Carignan is the backbone here — it brings the savory, mineral depth that younger-vine blends simply cannot replicate.
parsed.terroir_expression: The schist and limestone-clay soils of the Têt valley corridor drain well and stress the vines, concentrating flavors in the fruit. The Mediterranean climate delivers 2,500+ hours of sunshine annually with minimal rainfall — Carignan thrives under these conditions because it naturally resists drought stress better than many varieties. The altitude gradient from valley floor to lower slopes creates a temperature swing between warm days and cool nights that preserves acidity while building phenolic ripeness, which explains the 14.5% ABV without feeling jammy or hot.
parsed.vinification_summary: Lafage typically employs a combination of destemming and whole-cluster fermentation, with temperature control to protect aromatics during maceration. The blend is assembled after separate vinification by variety, allowing the winemaker to balance Syrah's peppery structure against Garnacha's warmth and Carignan's iron-mineral backbone. Oak aging is moderate — a portion in used French barrels to add texture without overwhelming the fruit. Carbonic maceration is sometimes used selectively on the Carignan component to soften its naturally aggressive tannins, which is why the wine drinks approachable young despite its structure.
food_pairing: Cassoulet with confited duck — the wine's earthy Carignan and iron notes cut through the rich pork fat, while the wine's warmth matches the dish's spice
Barcelona-style bravas with allioli — the wine's herbal depth and tannic grip stand up to fried potato richness without overwhelming the garlic
Lamb tagine with preserved lemon and green olives — Monastrell's dark fruit and the wine's garrigue notes complement North African spice profiles
Weeknight pasta with bolognese — the acidity lifts tomato richness while the body stands up to the meat's fat
Grilled merguez sausage with harissa yogurt — the wine's peppery Syrah component mirrors the sausage's spice while the tannin handles the fat
parsed.comparable_wines: Mas de Isard Côtes Catalanes — similar old-vine Carignan-dominant blend from the same appellation at comparable price; Côtes du Roussillon Villages Les Arènes from Mjt — fuller-bodied, more extracted take on Roussillon reds at $18-22; Badet-Clayette Côtes Catalanes Cuvée Montmajor — direct competitor at $13-15 with a rounder, less structured style
parsed.style_profile: Medium-full bodied dry red with firm-but-approachable tannins, dark fruit and garrigue aromatics, and a savory iron-mineral finish
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink now through 2022 at latest — the tannins are resolved enough to drink young but there's little benefit from further cellaring. Store at 55-60°F with minimal temperature fluctuation.
parsed.value_assessment: At $14.56 this undercuts comparable Côtes du Roussillon Villages wines by $4-8 and outpaces most of them in complexity. The LCBO pricing puts it against basic French table wines and Italian Pinot Grigio at the same price tier, which makes it an obvious choice for anyone seeking character over convenience. The only real competitor at this price with similar old-vine Carignan expression is the Badet-Clayette Montmajor.
parsed.market_position: This sits on LCBO shelves between French table wine and regional appellation wines — a sweet spot for adventurous home cooks and restaurant guests seeking something different without a sommelier's guidance. It moves in wine bars and casual dining restaurants that emphasize local and seasonal menus, where its food-friendliness and price point make it a reliable pour-by-the-glass option.
parsed.insider_take: Most buyers treat this as a casual everyday red and miss what makes it special — the old-vine Carignan expression is closer to Priorat than to basic Roussillon. If you're comparing it to Côtes du Rhône or basic Languedoc, you're looking at the wrong category. The tradeoff is straightforward: you get structure and terroir at the price of approachability — this rewards food and attention, not casual gulping.
